newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Armed police stationed in Cambodian garment factory.
newsitem.headline: Armed police stationed in Cambodian garment factory.

text.p: About 100 military police were stationed inside a Cambodian garment factory on Thursday after labour unrest erupted in violence outside the factory gates, workers said.
Workers from the Hong Kong-owned Tack Fat factory told Reuters that police, many holding AK-47s, stood watch over them as they worked.
About 500 of the Tack Fat's 1,000 workers reported for work on Thursday, with the rest striking or staying home, they said.
Earlier in the day, police fired shots in the air and threw punches at opposition leader Sam Rainsy and his deputy when they tried to encourage workers to join the strike, witnesses said.

Witnesses said Khieu Rada, secretary general of Sam Rainsy's officially unrecognised Khmer Nation Party (KNP), was punched repeatedly and his mouth was bleeding as police scuffled with several dozen strikers.
At least seven workers were slightly injured in the fracas, the witnesses said.
Sam Rainsy returned to the factory in the afternoon, but left quickly after police and a man in civilian clothes told him to go away. The man refused to identify himself.
King Norodom Sihanouk on Thursday expressed distress over the increasingly tense situation in annotations to a press release from Sam Rainsy.
He said he told Sam Rainsy not go too far in leading demonstrations because "the workers would risk losing everything if the capitalists were to close their factories."

Thursday's incident was the fourth protest at the Tack Fat factory and the ninth since December 10, when Sam Rainsy formed a union for garment workers. With 36 factories employing more than 16,000 workers, the garment sector is Cambodia's fastest-growing industry.
In the past week, the government has become increasingly forceful in shutting down Sam Rainsy, who has organised all of the recent strikes, as industry officials complain of cancelled orders.
On Saturday, police used fire hoses to break up one demonstration. On Wednesday and Thursday, they forced Sam Rainsy from the Tack Fat factory grounds.
Cambodian garment workers have complained of low pay, long hours and poor conditions, and human rights workers have called their work environment appalling.

Human rights observers said they were also concerned about what they perceived as forced union elections at Tack Fat and other factories. They said factory managers were electing puppet representatives to squelch complaints by workers.
Industry representatives said the union elections were free, and added that they had made broad, industry-wide concessions to workers effective January 1.
